name: Burundi
card_headline: President Ndayishimiye entered the May 2027 race with the opposition sidelined, while fuel scarcity, a two-to-one dollar gap and the Congo war strain the country
card_summary: The ruling CNDD-FDD holds every contested seat after the 2025 vote, and the presidential election is set for 3 May 2027. [1][2] FEWS NET put the parallel dollar near 6,000 francs against about 3,000 officially in February, with fuel up about 50 percent. [3] Critical Threats says about 18,000 Burundian troops were in the DRC in December 2025, and more than 6,000 remained in South Kivu by June. [4] About 230,000 Congolese refugees have arrived since 2025. [3]
card_local: Burundi Times reports five opposition parties asking the electoral commission to pause, and Burundi Eco reports doubled or tripled transport fares. Independent local reporting is thin in this draft. [5][6]
card_international: Reuters and AP report Burundi's agreement to take third-country deportees from the United States, and Africanews reports eleven parties backing the president. [7][8][9]
card_scholar: Critical Threats and Crisis Group track the army's role in the Congo war, ISS finds refugee returns from Tanzania coercive, and the IMF sees an overvalued official rate. [4][10][11][12]
context_md: Evariste Ndayishimiye has led Burundi, a country of about 15 million, since 2020, when he succeeded Pierre Nkurunziza after Nkurunziza's death. [2] The presidential term is seven years. [9] The 2005 Arusha Accord ended a civil war, and Human Rights Watch dates the decline in openness to the 2015 protests against Nkurunziza's third-term bid. [13] The Imbonerakure, the ruling party's youth league, appear in most reports of abuse. [13] From late 2021 Burundian troops entered South Kivu in the DRC to hunt the RED-Tabara rebels, who oppose Bujumbura and have Rwandan backing. [10] Burundi later closed its land border with Rwanda after accusing Kigali of backing that group. [14]

sections.title: One party holds every contested seat, and the May 2027 vote has a date, a candidate and few rivals
sections.body_md:
The ruling CNDD-FDD won 96.5 percent in the June 2025 legislative vote and took every contested seat in the National Assembly and Senate, along with nearly all commune council seats, according to Human Rights Watch. [1] HRW says opposition candidates were sidelined by legal and administrative means, and that observers, journalists and opposition representatives were kept out of some polling places. The African Union's preliminary report called the vote peaceful. [15]

The presidential vote is set for 3 May 2027. The electoral commission, CENI, announced the calendar on 8 May 2026, and its president, Prosper Ntahorwamiye, said the winner would be sworn in on 18 June 2027. [5][2] The campaign runs from 10 to 30 April. [16] The CNDD-FDD named Ndayishimiye its candidate on 26 April, and Africanews calls him the widely seen favourite. [16][2] Burundi Times listed his entry into the race on 13 November, and Africanews reports that nomination papers were due by 22 November, with a June runoff if no one wins an absolute majority. [17][9] No official candidate list was found for this draft.

The opposition is divided. Five parties (CNL, UPRONA, CODEBU, Sahwanya-Frodebu and CDP) asked CENI on 8 May to suspend preparations, citing irregularities in 2025, and the president replied on X that uneasy parties need "parental dialogue." [5] On 13 November eleven parties that Africanews calls opposition said they would run a joint campaign for him. Africanews does not name them. [9] CENI's projected budget is 115.8 billion francs, of which 3.8 billion was secured as of February. [5]

Critical Threats reports, from local media and unnamed sources, that Ndayishimiye is competing with party figure Révérien Ndikuriyo and that arrests since March 2026 may aim to remove rivals. It adds that critics see the FRAD reserve force as a way around Arusha power-sharing limits. [4] The Kofi Annan Foundation's electoral vulnerability index scores Burundi 84.6 and gives a 98.4 percent probability of electoral violence, against a regional baseline of 51.1. [18]

lenses.local: Burundi Times carries the opposition's joint statement and the president's reply; its November coverage was read by headline only. [5][17]
lenses.international: Africanews and KOACI report the calendar, the candidacy and the eleven-party endorsement. [2][16][9]
lenses.scholar: The Kofi Annan Foundation rates electoral violence risk at 98.4 percent, and Critical Threats describes an internal power struggle in the ruling party. [18][4]

sections.title: Fuel is scarce and the dollar costs about twice its official price
sections.body_md:
FEWS NET, in analysis current to 27 February 2026, reports that the fuel price rose about 50 percent after border closures with the DRC cut the informal imports Burundians used to resell. It expected shortages to last through September 2026 because of limited foreign exchange. It put the official rate near 3,000 francs to the dollar and the parallel rate near 6,000. [3] On 24 May Citizen Digital reported long queues at Bujumbura stations and quoted unnamed officials describing "unprecedented fuel scarcity," with no Burundian prices. [19] Burundi Eco's 10 July issue urged the government to act and to liberalise the fuel trade, and said transport fares had doubled or tripled, a claim it does not attribute. [6] A civil society forum describes police clearing Bujumbura bus parks because no buses ran, and fuel sold on a black market at much higher prices, with no figures and no date. [20]

The problem recurs. Iwacu's English archive lists fuel shortages in Bujumbura in 2017 and 2018 and a pump price of 2,250 francs per litre announced in January 2018. [21]

Official data are milder. The statistics institute INSBU, as reprinted by Burundi Eco, puts the first-quarter 2026 dollar average at 2,977.5 francs against 2,922.4 a year earlier, and inflation at 11.5 percent. Petroleum was the largest import category at 8.6 percent of imports, the trade deficit reached 798.6 billion francs, and the 2026-2027 budget law adds a road levy of 75 francs per litre. [6]

The IMF's June Article IV says growth was 4.2 percent in 2025 on coffee and gold exports. Inflation fell from 45 percent in April 2025 to 8.6 percent in April 2026 but is projected at 14.5 percent for 2026, and reserves were 213.9 million dollars, or 1.6 months of imports. The Fund says the official rate looks significantly overvalued, says the parallel premium is narrower without giving a figure, and urges a roadmap to a unified, flexible rate. It lists fiscal slippage before the 2027 elections among the risks, rates the risk of debt distress as high, and expects the Middle East war to have a limited near-term effect. [12]

lenses.local: Burundi Eco and FORSC report queues, black-market fuel and sharply higher fares, but neither gives pump or parallel dollar prices. [6][20]
lenses.international: Citizen Digital relays official descriptions of unprecedented scarcity and adds no figures. [19]
lenses.scholar: FEWS NET and the IMF are the main sources, and they differ on how wide the parallel dollar premium is. [3][12]

sections.title: The army in the Congo war: about 18,000 in December, more than 6,000 by June
sections.body_md:
The figure of about 18,000 comes from Critical Threats and describes December 2025. Its 12 December note said Burundi's army had begun withdrawing roughly 18,000 troops from South Kivu after M23 and Rwandan forces took Uvira, and that Burundi closed its two main border posts. [22] ACLED dates the capture to 10 December and notes that the lowland plain around Uvira had been held by Congolese and Burundian forces and allied armed groups. [23] Critical Threats' 1 September 2026 special edition cites security sources quoted by French media for at least 18,000 Burundian troops in the DRC in December 2025, and Jeune Afrique sources for more than 6,000 in South Kivu in mid-June 2026. It says Burundi closed the border for 10 weeks, redeployed from late December, and that M23 left the Ruzizi Plain in May under US pressure. [4] UNHCR dates the border reopening to 23 February. [24]

Crisis Group's 19 December report gives no total and says only that several battalions are in South Kivu. It cites reports of at least 20 Burundian soldiers killed in early December and says the Congolese army uses Bujumbura airport as a logistics hub, including for drones. [10] Burundi publishes no deployment or casualty figures. Critical Threats reports that at least six senior officers have died since November 2023 and that insider estimates of total deaths run from hundreds to thousands, and it flags these as unverified. It also reports, unverified, Congolese payments of up to 5,000 dollars per soldier and a gold-smuggling motive. [4] HRW reports that a military appeals court upheld heavy sentences in February 2025, some of them life terms, for 272 soldiers convicted in 2024 of refusing deployment. [1]

Rwanda's president Paul Kagame says more than 20,000 Burundian troops are fuelling the war, according to a New Times headline. The page seen carried no body text and no Burundian reply. [25] Crisis Group's 2026 priorities, as summarised by Burundi Times, warn of a "fully blown inter-state confrontation" without urgent diplomacy. [14] Ndayishimiye has chaired the African Union since 14 February 2026, and a New Times commentary built on three critics argues his army's role weakens him as a mediator. [26]

lenses.local: Burundi Times relays Crisis Group's warning and reports that Burundian officials called for stronger regional oversight of Rwanda's role. [14]
lenses.international: The New Times carries Kagame's 20,000 claim and a critical AU commentary, both from a Rwandan outlet. [25][26]
lenses.scholar: Critical Threats, ACLED and Crisis Group give the best sourced accounts of Uvira and the army's role, and none has an official troop figure. [4][23][10]

sections.title: Two refugee flows cross Burundi in opposite directions
sections.body_md:
FEWS NET counted about 230,000 Congolese refugees in Burundi in February 2026, more than 100,000 of whom arrived after 6 December 2025, with about 67,000 at the Busuma site. [3] UNHCR said on 23 March that more than 33,000 Congolese had gone home from Burundi in a month after the border reopened on 23 February, that about 109,000 remained, and that its Burundi refugee response was 20 percent funded. [24] UNHCR's 11 September update counts 2,084 returns in a two-week period and 18,232 assisted returns in total, and does not say how that total relates to the March figure. [27]

Not every return is free. HRW reports that in September 2025 police and Imbonerakure detained hundreds of Congolese refugees and asylum seekers and told them to go to a camp or return, and that Tutsi suspected of links to Rwanda or M23 faced discriminatory treatment, citing the UN Special Rapporteur. [1]

In the other direction, ISS reports that tens of thousands of Burundians have come home from Tanzania since December 2025, mainly from Nduta camp, which closed in April, with Nduta and Nyarugusu due to close by mid-2026, affecting about 142,000 people. ISS calls the returns coercive and politically timed ahead of 2027, says reintegration support is a one-off 150 dollars, and says opposition members and supporters fear persecution. [11] FEWS NET said food assistance for returnees would drop from three months to 45 days from March, and refugee rations stood at 75 percent. [3]

lenses.international: UNHCR reports falling funding and rising returns to Uvira and Fizi, where many returnees found homes looted or destroyed. [24]
lenses.scholar: ISS argues that returns from Tanzania risk another round of forced displacement. [11]

sections.title: Repression: arrests by police and youth league, and a press that works around the law
sections.body_md:
HRW cites UN experts who recorded at least 200 cases of sexual violence, 58 enforced disappearances, 62 acts of torture, 892 arbitrary detentions and 605 extrajudicial killings between January 2024 and May 2025, often involving state agents or their proxies. [1] SOS-Torture Burundi reports that on 6 July 2026 police and Imbonerakure arrested more than 80 men in Bujumbura in a "control operation," held them at the municipal police station, and that witnesses said they were suspected of having no job in the city. This rests on the monitor alone. [28] HRW also reports compulsory CNDD-FDD contributions of 1,000 to 5,000 francs per person since August 2024, enforced by threats and denial of public services. [1]

Speech about the economy is also policed. HRW says authorities reportedly ordered the Belgian development agency Enabel's country director to leave in September 2025 after he shared a LinkedIn cartoon about the fuel shortage. [1]

The press survives by working around restrictions. RSF reports that Willy Kwizera of Bonesha FM was arrested on 21 April 2025 and again on 28 April, when alleged Imbonerakure beat him, and that eight media heads condemned the violence on 3 May. Authorities did not answer RSF. [29] CPJ reports that journalist Sandra Muhoza, convicted of undermining territorial integrity and inciting ethnic hatred over comments in a WhatsApp group, was ordered provisionally released on 27 February 2026 after nearly two years and must stay in Ngozi province. [30] RSF recorded in 2022 that the Iwacu site was unblocked after five years. [31] SOS Médias Burundi began as an anonymous collective after radio stations were destroyed in May 2015, per RSF's 2016 profile. [32]

lenses.local: SOS-Torture Burundi documents arrests in Bujumbura week by week, and Burundi Times carried the joint opposition statement. [28][5]
lenses.international: RSF and CPJ document attacks on named journalists. [29][30]
lenses.scholar: HRW's World Report 2026 is the main consolidated account, drawing on UN Special Rapporteur findings. [1]

sections.title: Washington and Gitega: a deportee deal and mining agreements
sections.body_md:
On 29 September 2026 presidential spokesperson Nancy Ninette Mutoni announced at an event in Ngozi that Burundi will accept people deported by the United States who have no prior connection to the country. [8][7] Only people not accused of crime or terrorism links will be accepted, and no numbers, timing or financial terms were given. [7] Reuters reports that the US has sent such deportees to about half a dozen African countries, that Senate Democrats say the deals cost tens of millions of dollars and lack transparency, and that rights groups say they let Washington bypass court protections some deportees had won. A foreign ministry spokesperson said details were not yet available. [7] AP reports that a flight of about 70 people to Burundi, Rwanda and the Central African Republic was cancelled after a US appeals court ruling the week before. [8]

Critical Threats says Burundi signed mining deals with the US in March 2026 and wants deeper security and minerals ties, and argues that its exclusion from the US-backed Washington accords leaves its military role unaddressed. [4] No contract text or official announcement for the mining deals was found for this draft.

lenses.international: Reuters and AP carry the deportee announcement, and neither has a US government comment. [7][8]
lenses.scholar: Critical Threats links the minerals deals to Burundi's bid for US attention on the Congo war. [4]

sections.title: Food: prices 10 to 90 percent above average and a lean season that starts in September
sections.body_md:
FEWS NET found staple food prices in January 2026 between 10 and 90 percent above five-year averages, depending on place and crop. It expected prices to follow seasonal trends and to rise above both last year and the historical average from September, when the main lean season begins. [3] It classed the Eastern Lowlands, Northern Lowlands and Imbo Plains as Stressed (IPC phase 2) through September 2026, with pockets of Crisis (phase 3), and estimated that 750,000 to 999,999 people would need urgent assistance, with needs peaking in April and May. [3] Fuel scarcity cut incomes and market access in the Imbo Plains, where many people earn a living from transport. [3] WFP resources covered about 75 percent of refugees' minimum food needs through April. [3]

Burundi Eco adds that transport fares have doubled or tripled and that entrepreneurs have turned to the black market for fuel. [6] No FEWS NET update after February was opened for this draft, so the post-September outlook is not covered.

lenses.local: Burundi Eco reports fare increases and black-market fuel purchases by businesses. [6]
lenses.scholar: FEWS NET is the main source on prices and phases and its analysis predates the lean season. [3]

Burundian troops enter South Kivu to hunt RED-Tabara rebels.

Police and Imbonerakure detain hundreds of Congolese refugees and asylum seekers.

scores.coverage_basis: Reuters and AP file on Burundi mainly when a deal or date lands, such as the 30 September deportee announcement. [7][8] Think tanks produce steady work on the Congo war and refugees. [4][10][11] I found no recent wire story on the fuel crisis, and local press output is constrained by repression. [19][29]

severity.basis: UN experts counted 605 extrajudicial killings and 892 arbitrary detentions from January 2024 to May 2025, and the army fights in South Kivu with unacknowledged losses. [1][4] There is no large internal armed conflict, so the score reflects state violence and the external war.
FEWS NET estimated 750,000 to 999,999 people would need urgent assistance, and about 230,000 Congolese refugees sit alongside returnees from Tanzania. [3][11]

The ruling party holds every contested seat, and journalists such as Sandra Muhoza have been jailed for months. [1][30] Kofi Annan Foundation gives a 98.4 percent probability of electoral violence. [18]
Fuel rose about 50 percent and the parallel dollar is near twice the official rate, with reserves at 1.6 months of imports and a high risk of debt distress. [3][12]
Inflation fell sharply and the deficit is narrowing, but fuel scarcity persisted through 2026, the war reached Uvira and the electoral field narrowed. [12][3][4]

parts.basis: The United States has a deportee deal and mining agreements with Burundi, and Rwanda and the DRC are drawn into the same rivalry. [7][4]
Exports are led by coffee and gold from a small economy with 1.6 months of import cover. [12]
Crisis Group warns the Burundi-Rwanda rivalry could become direct conflict, and Congolese refugees have crossed in large numbers. [10][14][3]
About 230,000 Congolese refugees are in Burundi and tens of thousands of Burundians are returning from Tanzania. [3][11]
Ndayishimiye chairs the African Union while his army fights in the DRC, and Burundi joins the US third-country deportation scheme. [26][7]

summary: Burundi matters beyond its borders mainly through the Congo war, the rivalry with Rwanda and refugee movements, not through trade. [10][4][3]
gi.up: A direct Burundi-Rwanda clash, an attack on Bujumbura airport, or a disputed May 2027 result.
gi.down: A durable ceasefire in South Kivu and a reopened Rwanda border.

gaps: Local sourcing is thin. Iwacu's recent output could not be reached: only 2017 to 2019 archive pages were opened, so no current Iwacu article is cited.

SOS Médias Burundi, Radio Publique Africaine, Bonesha FM and Burundi Daily sites could not be opened. They appear here only through RSF and CPJ, and SOS Médias only through a 2016 RSF profile, so none supplies direct local reporting.
RTNB and ABP pages were not opened, so no state_affiliated source is cited and the official line on fuel and the election is missing.
Burundi Times pages other than two articles were read by headline only.
No Reuters, AP or AFP story on the fuel and forex collapse in the last 90 days was found; fuel claims rest on FEWS NET (February), Citizen Digital (May), Burundi Eco (July) and an undated FORSC note.
FEWS NET and the IMF differ on the size of the parallel dollar premium, and no current parallel rate was found.
Troop figures come from unnamed security sources through French media, as reported by Critical Threats, and no official figure exists.
The CENI candidate list, validation date and the names of the eleven parties backing the president were not located.
The refugee section has no local source. UNHCR's March and September return counts use different bases.
Critical Threats and Crisis Group documents were read only in part (first 100,000 characters).
No ACLED Burundi event data was opened, so violence scoring relies on HRW and UN figures.
No documentary or film was verified (media list is empty), and the DW podcast episode has no visible date.
Rio Times pages on Burundi were found but not cited because they were produced by an automated newsroom.
The IMF Article IV staff report and Crisis Group's own 2026 priorities page were not opened.
